Mark Larmour: As part of the talks that led to the New D ecade, New A pproach agreement , there was a strong line of discussion and much work done around transparency . Part of that came out of the context of the renewable heat incentive , which was one of the factors in the background to the instability at the time the Executive collapsed . Much work has been done by the parties , which then fed into the final text that was agreed in New Decade, New Approach .

Proposals to change the Ministerial code and the code under which spads work have been implemented by the Department of Finance as part of that. They have been brought forward for the Assembly to take forward as well. We are able to share our experience in the UK Government of how civil servants work alongside special advisers with Ministers, et cetera, as part of that process. That was a very in-depth and effective strand of conversation as part of the talks that fed into the final text that was created for New Decade, New Approach , as set out in the chapter in annexe A on transparency and the accountability of the Executive .

Q68 Claire Hanna: I know we have a lot of ground to cover , so I just want to finish on this. Are there other reforms that you think are required and how will you measure success with the reforms that have been brought in?

The key measure of success for all of this is going to be the sustainability of the E xecutive and the Assembly. It also very much comes back to the context in which the New Decade, New Approach deal was reached , and the fact that it is delivering on the priorities of the people in Northern Ireland. We have seen some real progress made on the health front and on addressing some of th os e upfront challenges that we we re facing back in January , but clearly there are other areas. There are some aspects of the institutional changes that clearly have not been tested yet , like the workings of an Opposition, something that was strengthened from the previous agreements on that.

We need to keep monitoring it . There is a role for the Secretary of State and indeed for the party leaders’ forum in monitoring how these institutional changes are working and making sure that they are working effectively. In that respect, we think there will be benefit from the introduction of an independent fiscal council. The work that the OBR does in the UK context is important. There are equivalent organisations in Scotland and the Republic of Ireland, and having an institution of that nature would be beneficial. That is an issue fundamentally for the Executive to take forward , but we are keen to see that established because we think i t could also help in supporting the Assembly and the Executive to do things more effectively.
Claire Hanna: That is an issue I would want to get on to , but I am aware that others want in, so that is it from me for now.

Q69 Mini s ter, you have noted in your answers the distorting effect of th e election i n Dublin and then Covid as well. When we return to normality, it is very important that we do not fall into the trap of saying, “Hang on, this New Decade, New Approach thing has been going for 10, 11 or 12 months and everything must be fine and dandy”, when i n actual fact there is likely to be a build-up of tensions, problems and arguments that have been put aside while the focus has been on Covid. We just need to be alert to that. Can you just give us any comfort that Dublin, you r office, and the offices of the First Minister and Deputy First Minister have that pencilled into your thinking?

Again , Chair, you make a very good point . We all recognise that there have been political events: we only had our election in December; we have had the long period of formation of an Irish Government , as you say; we have had the extremely welcome coming together of the Executive; and then we have had the impact of Covid on all this. Legislative timetables, in particular, have been affected by that.

We need to lea n into delivery of the package. It is important in that context, as the deal was very clear in its preamble, that this was not just about getting the devolved institutions back up and running ; i t was about making sure that they delivered for the people of Northern Ireland. In that respect, the progress that has been made on the health front is very welcome. In other areas , such as integrating education , there is a lot more work to be done. On the economy, we were off to quite a good start with the work on city deals , growth deals and that side of things but, clearly, there is a massive challenge now for the economy to support the recovery post-Covid in Northern Ireland. It will require all parties and all the Governments to be at the top of their game to address that .

Yes, there will need to be a renewed sense of urgency, as you say, when things get back to normal. None of us know s exactly when that will be just yet , but our priorities as a Department are to keep driving this process forward and to use the machinery that the deal has set up to ensure that is delivered across the whole piece .

Q70 Can I suggest a management of expectations among the communities not to lose faith in this document because Covid has been a distorter? We will price it into our thinking. It is important that everybody else does as well. I am sure you would agree.

I very much agree with that. I would just observe on that front that one area where I have already seen that in action is in the conversations we have been having about legacy and the legislation , which was originally envisaged to be in place within 100 days . We have seen recognition across victims’ groups and across communities that it is more important to get the detail right than it is to do this quickly. That is absolutely right . It is still a priority on which we want to move forward , but it is really important to get it right and to do it properly .

Q71 Scott Benton: Good morning, Minister. Thank you for joining us. The agreement stated that the UK Government would work in conjunction with parties in the Executive to thrash out the precise details of the financial support package. How many discussions have you had with the parties i n the E xecutive since January on these issues? Assuming you have spoken with those parties since March, has Covid-19 influenced the longer - term approach to finances in Northern Ireland?

Thank you for the question. As I mentioned earlier, I was not in the room for the negotiations leading up to the deal. Julian is probably the best-placed person to tell you about the detail of that, as I know he already has. I have met with Ministers from all the parties in the Executive over the last few months . Indeed, I have been in touch with some of them very regularly , partly as part of the Covid response .

There are some things that the funding we provided through the deal has already unblocked and allowed to move forward, such as the funding for health and addressing the nurses’ pay dispute, which are really crucial and very welcome. There are others where it has perhaps had that indirect effect. I mentioned earlier the match fund ing for the inclusive future fund , where the UK Government made a significant commitment but the match fund ing from the Executive will make a real difference to the ability of that to deliver.

As Julian said, the £2 billion package we put forward is the biggest deal for a Northern Ireland talks process of its kind . It adds on to the over £1 billion a month that was already due to be spent in Northern Ireland . It provide s substantial resource and capital funding to get things moving forward. It would not surprise you to hear that many of the Ministers I speak to would always want more . We recognise that that is part of the mature relationship that exists between a Government and a devolved Government, and part of the discussions that we will always have.

I t is important to recognise that there have been separate Barnett consequentials as a result of Covid, in the region of £1.3 billion for Northern Ireland. That, of course, is welcome and necessary, and I would not suggest that that was anything other than necessary . It is also really important that, as we look at the opportunities for recovery, there are areas where the UK Government can help on this front. The Northern Ireland Office will always be making the case for them to do as much as they can . We need to recognise the substantial nature of the financial package that was agreed as part of this deal and the fact that that has been able to kick-start a good deal of change.

Q72 Scott Benton: I am conscious that you were not in the room when the agreement was thrashed out . I appreciate that is the case but, out of interest, the exact level of funding and the calculations that underpin the £2 billion funding package were not discussed with the parties before the deal was published. Do you think that process has caused any friction in your subsequent discussions with the parties in the Executive , or any friction with the UK Government , because that was the approach taken when the deal was published?

The allocation of the £ 2 billion was announced days after the deal was reached. I remember at the time, when we established within the Department that that was likely to be the figure , there was a degree of optimism within the Department that it would be very well received , which was immediately pushed back on when some Northern Irish politicians began to speak about substantially larger figures that they might have wanted. That is somewhat in the nature of the relationship between the Government and the devolved G overnment , and will always be part of the challenge.

We need to look at what the money was for and how those figures were reached. If I break down the figure of the £2 billion, there was a £1 billion Barnett-based investment guarantee from the UK Government to include significant new funding to turbocharge infrastructure investment. That was guaranteed to apply in all circumstances —so not just money that might have been coming anyway , but a clear guarantee over five years that that money would come through so that the Executive could plan investment over a five-year period.

There is then around £245 million for the support of the transformation of public services, including across health, education and justice. Of that £ 245 million , £ 44 million has already been made available with the rest allocated over the next four years. There was a rapid injection of £550 million to put the Executive’s finances on a sustainable footing. That included £200 million over three years to resolve the nurses’ pay dispute , something that everyone would welcome, particularly in the context of Covid.

Alongside this, there was the offer from the UK G overnment of £60 million of capital and resource funding to deliver the Northern Ireland graduate ‑ entry medical school in Derry/Londonderry, which has since been approved by the Executive and should now be able to go ahead . There was £ 50 million for the rollout of ultra-low emission public transport and half of that is available in the current year. Then there was £140 million to address Northern Ireland’s unique circumstances.
These are substantial commitments that we were able to make. That breakdown reflects the fact that we had robust discussions with the Treasury in getting to them.

Q73 Scott Benton: As well as the British Government’s investment, as part of the deal, the Irish Government also pledged infrastructure support for cross-border transport projects . Clearly, a lot has happened since January in terms of Covid-19 and the political nuances around the formation of a new Government . Do you have any reason to doubt that the Irish Government will be able to fulfil those pledges because of what has happened since?

No . Coming back to the Chair’s opening remarks about the statements they have made, the fact that they have put New Decade, New Approach at the centre of those statements and committed to it show s that they want to come up to the plate with regard to these. One interesting area to explor e is connectivity , which, both within the UK but also north-south, may be one of the opportunities to support Northern Ireland in the Covid recovery. We would welcome them potentially going further than some of the commitments that have been made to date. We are comfortable that these are commitments that they can meet and, as far as we can see, fully intend to meet.

Q74 Scott Benton: To go back to the issue we have just spoken about , the finances of the Executive , there seems to be a clear political consensus in Northern Ireland, potentially espoused best by the Finance Minister in his comments on the funding that is or is not available, as he may well put it. In relation to Covid-19, which we have just touched on, and the wider questions on UK public finances, when do you think there may be a time to revisit the £2 billion package and how likely do you think that will be as part of those broader discussions with the Treasury going forward?

The package related to N ew D ecade , N ew A pproach is the package. It is what was agreed as a five-year package with that upfront element of addressing immediate challenges for public services. The Executive is being adequately funded to support its commitments. Under the deal, we provided a £2 billion financial package, which is the biggest single package to support a talks deal in well over a decade. It addresses the key priorities identifie d by the parties during talks: supporting sustainable budgeting, helping to transform public services, turbocharging infrastructure investment and addressing Northern Ireland’s unique circumstances.

When something like Covid comes along, you have to be able to provide extra funding and support. We have done that through £ 1.3 billion so far in B arnet t consequentials on that front, which is of course additional to the £2 billion provided through this support.

It is part of the Northern Ireland Office’s role to look at where we can add value, including with the Covid recovery process, and ensure that that is pr operly funded. It is something we will always engage in, but that is not to say that we want to reopen the package that was agreed for New D ecade, New A pproach . That is the package that is there. That is what is being delivered and a substantial part of it has already been delivered. We are seeing real changes as a result of that and I welcome that.
Q75 Minister, are you able to confirm whether there will be consequentials to Northern Ireland as a result of the announcement with regards to free school meals yesterday?

I have asked our officials about this . I see that a number of the industrious members of your Committee have already been tweeting about that. I have not had the answer yet , but logically I would have thought that there would be.
Q76 You would be making the case to Treasury that that should be the case.
Of course , but I am awaiting further in f o rmation on that front . I cannot absolutely 100% confirm that that is the decision we make, but it seems to me that that would make sense.
Q77 Ian Paisley: Would HMG be paying for it instead of the Executive? Is that what the Minister is telling us?
No, I am saying that there would be Barnett consequentials of a decision reached about this in England.
Q78 There will be a B arnet t consequential through to the Executive following the decision of the Government yesterday .
That is my assumption but, as I say, I have asked for more detail and I have yet to hear back. I will write to you if there is any change to that.

Minister, we are grateful to you for that. If there is anything this Committee can do to strengthen your elbow, just shout, as they say. I turn to Mr Farry, who is not going to shout. He is going to ask his question in sweet and dulcet tones.

Stephen Farry: Still on the issue of finances, I welcome the financial package and acknowledge what the Minister has said , that that is the package in relation to New Decade, New Approach. I just want to make a couple of points and ask a question on this.
In the interest of time, can we have a question rather than a point ?

Q79 Stephen Farry: Bearing in mind that the Northern Ireland public finances were unsustainable prior to New Decade, New Approach—it is important to recognise and acknowledge that—that Covid has knocked the budget in Northern Ireland significantly off course and that the New Decade, New Approach mon e y s of themselves were not going to address all the aspirations the Executive had, t o what extent can the Northern Ireland O ffice work with the E xecutive to re - profile some of the commitments and to support the reform package in particular?

The difficulty we have, Minister, is that , unless we are able to reform health and education, Northern Ireland public finances are not going to be sustainable in the long term. The difficulty is that the amount of money for transformation to get to a sustainable point will require some additional funding. We are caught in this dilemma where we cannot go forward and we cannot go backwards ; we are still treading water and N ew D ecade , New Approach does not really enable us to break out of that cycle. To w hat extent do you see a more difficult financial situation facing the Executive ? Is there scope to work in partnership , by giving challenges and requiring commitments from the Executive , to make our finances more sustainable , particularly around health and education?

You are right to refer to the importance of working in partnership on these issues. The deal itself did provide that rapid injection, which recognised the challenges that the Executive had faced with sustainability , and £550 million in that respect is not a small amount of money.

We also have to recognise that public spending per head in Northern Ireland is the highe st of any UK region. Last year, before this additional funding, it was around 20% above the UK average. That needs to be put on a more sustainable footing. There is a role for the UK Government in supporting that process and we will continue to work with the Executive as the Northern Ireland Office to make the case f or investment that can save wherever necessary. There is also a real role for the A ssembly and the E xecutive to take responsibility on some of these issues .

That is why we think having an independent fiscal council to advise them with credibility could really help. In the UK context, all parties recognise that the OBR provides a useful function in that respect . Something along those lines in Northern Ireland to provide the information and some of the challenge could be really helpful to that process.

Q80 Stephen Farry: To come back on that, Chair, you will notice I worked it all into my question. Would the Minister think that there is a case to be made to Treasury, for example, for some additional borrowing powers for the Executive ? In terms of direct cash resource transfers, the situation is more limited. To what extent is there scope for creativity to give that greater degree of latitude for reforms, albeit with strict conditions given from Treasury around delivery , in terms of actually delivering reforms in Northern Ireland for once?

I am always happy to engage with Treasury colleagues on these issues. As you say, they are always inclined to put on pretty strict conditions when it comes to these things. Having the extra support and the credibility provided by an independent fiscal council could be helpful to the Executive in supporting those conversations.

We also need to recognise that there are already revenue-raising powers available to the E xecutive that, in many cases , for political reasons, they have chosen not to use. There needs to be a long-term conversation about how to put the Executive on a financially sustainable footing. We will absolutely support that and will do any engagement with the Treasury that is required on that front.

It is also important to recognise that the Northern Ireland Office itself is a relatively small organisation without a huge budget to dis bu rse. It is not like we necessarily have resources of our own that we can put into this process.

Q81 Stephen Farry: We always welcome NIO M inisters batting for Northern Ireland and standing up for us. As a party that has always been open to considering revenue raising, I would make the qualification that, in the current Covid recovery situation, increasing any revenue on households is incredibly difficult. While , in theory , that may well be a route, the borrowing route, given that the Chancellor is a little more open to increasing borrowing, may be the route to go and part of any viable pathway for the Executive .

I am sure your C hair would not object to me noting that this current coronavirus crisis is making good Keynesians out of us all . In that respect, I have no problem with that personally and I suspect the Chair does not either.
Minister, as always , you are prescient in your assessment.

Q82 Claire Hanna: The old li n e that everyone is a Keynesian in a foxhole has never felt more real. Some of us already were Keynesians and, like Stephen Farry said, there would be real opportunities. Some may say that we have not dealt particularly well with the fiscal powers that we currently have but certainly there would be opportunities for the Executive.

You spoke about the independent fiscal council and about opportunities to improve the long-term sustainability. Would you propose that the UK Government would be responsible for appointing members to that?

First and foremost, the composition of the independent fiscal council is for the Executive to decide on. If they were to ask us to provide support and to potentially put people on to it, of course we would look at that. It is pretty clear, certainly on my reading of the agreement, that it is in the hands of the Executive to decide on that. The crucial thing is its independence. It needs to demonstrate independence from the UK Government and Her Majesty’s Treasury as well as from the Department of Finance.

In that respect, some important work has been done by the OECD as to what makes for effective independent fiscal councils that contribute to better fiscal outcomes. To work effectively, they need to be genuinely independent and have timely access to all the information required to make their assessments. The joint board will want to ensure that it agrees on the terms of reference for a new institution . It will also want to make sure that the appointment of a director is done on the basis of merit and technical competence through a transparent process. Consideration also needs to be given to safeguards. With regards to OBR appointments, for instance, there is actually a role for the Treasury Select Committee.

F irst and foremost , we would like to see proposals from the Executive as to how they see this running . If there is a role for us where we can help , we are not insisting on a nomination right , but we would be happy to support the process.

Q83 Ian Paisley: The Government commissioned a report into the union by a peer and it was to be published last year. I am wondering if there are any relevant findings in that document that play into the responsibilities in making this new agreement actually work. With the Minister’s responsibilities with regards to making devolution work and with his interests in the union, is he prepared to share any of those findings with us or indeed even publish the document?
Sorry, I may have missed part of your question, Ian. I was not clear what report you were referring to.
Ian Paisley: It was a peer from the House of Lords. I cannot quite remember his name.
Was it Lord Bew ?
Ian Paisley: No, it was not Lord Bew . There was a report commissioned on the union .
It was Lord Dunlop.

Q84 Ian Paisley: That is the report. I wonder if any of the findings contained in that report are relevant to New Decade, New Approach and to its implementation. Do the Government ever intend to publish that report or share its findings with us?

I am happy to take that away and look at it because I remember talking to Lord Dunlop as part of his report. At the time I was sitting in both the Northern Ireland Office and the Scotland Office . I helped to provide evidence and support to him on that. That review was commissioned by and to the Cabinet Office , so it would have responsibility for any details around the publication. I am very happy to go away and ask those questions and to come back to you with a response on that.
Ian Paisley: That would be very helpful and very useful. I am sure there are implications, potentially, for the agreement and the future relationships.
Mr Paisley , I think I heard you say that that Dunlop review has not been put into the public domain. I do not recall seeing it. Do you?
Ian Paisley: It has not been published yet, Chair , and the Minister has told us that it is a Cabinet Office responsibility . We would be asking to have it published.

W e are seeing the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster tomorrow . We will certainly write to the Cabinet Office as well but perhaps, Minister, you could undertake to do anything that you can to aid that. Likewise, at some point, we will need a little extra information with regards to the operation of the new unit of the union operating within No. 10. I would guess that that draw s quite s ignificantly on the Dunlop review. That is all fine and dandy but, if we do not know what the Dunlop review says, we cannot really assess whether it is being successful. Thank you .
Did you have any other questions, Mr Paisley, with regards to the joint board?

Q85 Ian Paisley: Unless the M inister has anything to tell us about the intention for when it meet s or its agenda , I imagine it has probably been overtaken by Covid and will be kick-started later on. The Minister may want to update us on the joint board proposal .

T o be honest, you are spot on. There was a scheduled meeting of the joint board on 26 March 20 20. It was hoped that that would be the first formal meeting but, understandably, a decision was taken to postpone that discussion to enable the Executive to focus on the vital work of responding to Covid ‑ 19. The Secretary of State agreed with the First Minister and the Deputy First Minister that structured work to implement the deal would be paused to allow us to focus completely on tackling the virus.

We have kept that position under review. We are very keen to get on with implementation now and will, as soon as possible, restart discussions with the Executive about a joint board and implementation. While present circumstances have made progress difficult, we absolutely recognise that people want to see movement. As we head into the recovery phase, working together on Covid-19 will hopefully be a real opportunity to take some of these issues forward . It is a priority to get that next meeting of the joint board scheduled but it has not been done yet.

Q86 Ian Paisley: I assume it is similar for the North South Ministerial Council and for the east west ministerial council: that all of this has really been put on hold. It is potentially an opportunity to look with fresh eyes at what is actually relevant to making the lives of people different, especially if the Dunlop review has anything in it .

Yes, that is right . I t is very important that , in that respect , we deliver on the broader union strategy for involving all parts of the UK most effectively. That is certainly a priority for both me and Brandon. I know that you will be able to quiz him on that tomorrow.

With regard to the N orth S outh M inisterial C ouncil —and this was mentioned in the Irish Government’s announcement that the Chair referred to at the beginning of his comments — I recognise that that is a matter for the Executive to take forward with the Irish Government and not a matter for us.

Ian Paisley: Yes, it is important, Minister, that the lines are not blurred going forward—I think you made this point in your opening comments— in the three-stranded approach, which has served the demarcation lines quite well.
Yes, absolutely .
Q87 Minister, is the joint board merely advisory or is it going to have decision-making powers?

The joint board is there to oversee. To some extent, it depends on exactly what you mean by decision-making powers. If the board reaches a decision, it is likely to then feed that decision back to the UK Government or the Executive in saying, “This needs to be got on with and this needs to be prioritised as an issue”, or, “This is a matter of concern” . It is not, however, there to direct spending decisions of the Government or the Executive . It is there to oversee the process and ensure that we are working together to deliver progress on the whole five-year package of New Decade, New Approach.

The answer to the distinction between advisory and decision - making is perhaps a l it tle more complicated than that but it is a board that is there to oversee the process. Obviously, it allows for co-ordination at the highest level between the Secretary of State, the First Minister and the Deputy First Minister.

Q88 Sorry, let me just explore that very briefly. It will obviously meet. It will discuss, review and monitor. It can urge and it can exhort. It cannot take any decisions . If its urgings and exhortations are listened to but ignored, de facto it is toothless . Its efficacy is based on mutual good will.

When we think about who is on that board , it is representing the chief figures : the Secretary of State, in the case of my Department , and the First Minister and Deputy First Minister on the Executive. I do not see any prospect of it being ignored. Decisions that they reach together or views that they take together are likely to become priorities for their respective organisations. In that respect, this is an important board to get up and running , and to have its input into the review.

I would not want to imply that this is in some way a mechanism by which the UK was taking responsibility over Executive decisions or vice versa. Responsibilities of the Governments are what they are and, within this, the board is there to encourage co-ordination between them and deliver y on the aims of the deal.

Having very regular conversations and engagement is important to assess progress. Of course, those regular conversations and engagement between the people on this board are taking place in the context of the current crisis. I know Brandon has been engaging very regularly on this with his counterparts in the Executive through Covid forums and through the quad, involving the Irish Government in terms of the Covid response .

Q89 Are we in danger of having such a multiplicity of quads and boards , and this, that and the other, that it creates opportunities to kick the difficult into the long grass, to pass the buck and to say, “The meeting to discuss this conven es in three months’ time and we cannot move forward until then” ? This strikes to the heart of a question I asked earlier. The people of Northern Ireland are utterly fed up to the back teeth of political process. They want to see the products of politic s : better education, better health, better housing, a buoyant economy, et cetera . Are you confident that , as welcome as the N ew D ecade , N ew A pproach documentation is , et cetera, everybody is seized of the need to deliver that?

That comes back to the core of what this deal is about. You hit the nail on the head . It was about getting devolution back up and running , but also getting the focus on the priorities of people in Northern Ireland. That is much more than just a process; that is about ensuring that the real priorities are taken forward and delivered on. A lot of progress has been made on that front as a result of the deal. We have seen the ending of the nurses’ dispute. We have seen extra money flowing into health and education in Northern Ireland. We see a huge opportunity , with the abilities of the UK Government and the Executive to work together in delivering growth deals and city deals to support the economy. That is even more important in the current Covid recovery context.

I absolutely agree that this is about focusing on the issues that matter to people, which are between multiple different parties and more than one Government . You need some degree of process to manage that and, in that respect, what has been set out in terms of the joint board is entirely reasonable , given the situation that was envisaged when this deal was reached. The fact that other circumstances have intervened in the meantime does not mean in any way that the delivery of the objectives of the deal are any less urgent , but it puts up obstacles to the practical working of the processes.
Q90 Do you see the agreement as static or organic?

The agreement itself , of course, is static. It was formed at a moment in time , but it focuses on issues, challenges and things that we need to continue to work together effectively on. Those are issues that are key priorities for the Northern Ireland Office and, from everything I have seen, are also key priorities for the parties in the Executive . Some difficult political decisions have to be taken along the way . This agreement provides a structural framework for allowing those to be taken and for reinforcing the stability of the Executive, but it is still the responsibility of the politicians , both in the UK and in Northern Ireland, to take those decisions and to get on with delivering.

Q91 Stephen Farry: To pick up on the most recent discussion , there was an expectation that a quarterly implementation report would be issued and I do not think we have had that , for understandable reasons. Are we likely to see an implementation report and a rep rogrammed timetable in the near future , for New Decade, New Approach ?

Y ou are right, of course. The original deal suggested that the first implementation meeting would have to take place at the end of January. For various reasons , that did not take place at the end of January and, as we said, the meetings of the board had to be postponed from March . Getting that report commissioned and properly progressed is a priority . It will require the implementation of a review meeting to take place with the respective representatives of the UK Government and the Executive . That is a priority for us as soon as such meetings can tak e place. I cannot promise a date for publication as yet , but we recognise that this is an important part of the deal and something that needs to be brought forward at the earliest opportunity . Mark, do you have anything more to add on that front?

Mark Larmour: I will just reinforce what the Minister has said. We want to have regular implementation meetings, looking at all the progress that has been made against each of the objectives in the New Decade, New Approach deal. We hope to have those every six months. As was said throughout this conversation, frankl y, the timetable has been thrown out of kilter by Covid. One of the earliest things that I want to do with the team in the NIO is to agree a timescale for those regular meetings along with supporting Ministers in setting up the joint board and other oversight matt ers.

A more general point is that we can never have enough contact between the various parties, the Executive and the UK Government around the delivery of these agreements. That has been a barrier to progress in the past , frankly. We are very keen to have the frameworks that we have set out during the course of this meeting in place and working to allow us to secure the commitments that have been made in this agreement as soon as possible.

Q92 Stephen Farry: If we turn our minds back to Stormont House, Mark has been here long enough to remember that. There was an implementation group that met after Stormont House almost on a weekly basis but then it very quickly petered out, and I think that contributed to Stormont House just going off the rails . There is a key lesson there that Mark has highlighted .

Mark Larmour: Y es, we did get into a pattern of six-monthly implementation review meetings involving all the parties, the UK Government and the Irish Government to look at progress across the board after Stormont House . We built fresh start commitments into that process . The last meeting of that particular process was in December 2016, just prior to the collapse of the Executive . We very much want to restart that process where we look at all the commitments that have been made in the various agreements within Stormont House, fresh start and now in New Decade, New Approach , and make sure that we are collectively reminding ourselves of the progress that needs to be made and marking achievements that have been made in the previous period.

As the M inister indicated, we want to get to a posit i on where we can have those meetings as soon as possible. We just need to work out what the timetable is, given the impact of Covid and certain other moving parts around that.

Thank you very much indeed . Minister and Mr La r mour, on behalf of the Committee, can I thank you for appearing before us today? We have had a few more technical issues than we have had on previous occasions, so apologies for that , but it has been a very useful session .

I would just close, Minister, if I may, by drawing the key thing. You are clearly focused, as is the Committee and, as we understand, all members of Stormont, on the need to nurture this process and support it where and how we can. We must all remain resolutely focused on delivery to improve the lives of those who live in Northern Ireland , and to not get so hogtied by process , review and all the rest of it where people lose faith in the process. By golly, their faith in the process of devolved governance has taken a very significant knock over the last three years.

I am certainly encouraged, and I hope colleagues on the Committee are as well, by the fact that you appear to be very seized of that challenge to do all you can to ensure that things move forward and that we see proper delivery, of course with the support of Her Majesty’s Treasury, which is always useful . T hank you again for attending. Can I thank colleagues for their input and contribution?
